topic: Black-box test design: equivalence classes and boundaries
title: Boundary values first, then the code
instructions:
## Design the tests from the specification

Specification: `grade(score)` returns `"A"` for 80 to 100, `"B"` for 70 to 79, `"C"` for 60 to 69, `"D"` for 50 to 59, `"F"` for 0 to 49, and raises `ValueError` for anything outside 0 to 100 or not a whole number.

## Do this

1. Write `boundary_cases()` returning the list of scores a boundary-value analysis demands: each boundary and the values just inside and outside it. It must include at least `-1, 0, 1, 49, 50, 59, 60, 69, 70, 79, 80, 99, 100, 101`.
2. Write `grade(score)` to the specification. The checks run it on your boundaries and on a few more.
hints: Boundaries are where the behaviour changes: 0, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 100. Test each with its neighbours.
if not isinstance(score, int) or isinstance(score, bool) or score < 0 or score > 100: raise ValueError(...)
Compare from the top down: if score >= 80: return "A", elif score >= 70 ...

checks.label: boundary_cases covers every boundary and its neighbours
checks.script:
cases = set(boundary_cases())
needed = {-1, 0, 1, 49, 50, 59, 60, 69, 70, 79, 80, 99, 100, 101}
missing = needed - cases
assert not missing, f"boundary cases missing: {sorted(missing)}"

checks.label: grade follows the specification at the boundaries
checks.name: grade

realityNote: Writing the boundary list before the code is the discipline that catches the off-by-one that would otherwise ship. In pytest each case becomes a parametrised test; the list you wrote is the parameter table.
